description: Apple scab is a serious fungal disease affecting Malus species worldwide, causing dark olive-green velvety lesions on leaves and scabby blemishes on fruit.
Black rot causes frogeye leaf spots, cankers on branches, and firm rotting of fruit often beginning at the calyx end.
A heteroecious rust requiring both apple trees and eastern red cedar/juniper trees to complete its complex two-year life cycle.
Foliage exhibits vigorous chlorophyll pigmentation, uniform leaf margins, and absence of fungal, bacterial, or necrotic lesions.
Common rust produces airborne spores that travel long distances on air currents, causing widespread brick-red pustules on upper and lower leaf surfaces.
A devastating fungal disease favoring moderate temperatures and humid conditions, producing large cigar-shaped necrotic lesions that reduce photosynthesis.
Healthy maize foliage featuring erect, dark green leaves with clean midribs and no lesions, blight, or nutrient deficiency signs.
Black rot is one of the most destructive grape diseases in warm, humid climates, capable of destroying up to 80% of clusters if unchecked.
A complex trunk disease causing 'tiger-stripe' interveinal chlorosis/necrosis on leaves and dark specks on berries, often leading to vine apoplexy (sudden wilt).
Healthy grapevine foliage displaying vibrant palmate green leaves without chlorosis, powdery efflorescence, or lesions.
Early blight affects potato foliage and tubers, causing characteristic dark target-patterned concentric rings primarily starting on older lower leaves.
Historically infamous as the pathogen behind the Irish Potato Famine, late blight is an aggressive oomycete that can devastate an entire field in days under cool, wet conditions.
Vigorous potato foliage with dense green compound leaves, sturdy stems, and no visible spotting or blight symptoms.
Bacterial spot is a widespread disease in warm, rainy climates, causing water-soaked leaf spots, defoliation, and unmarketable scabby fruit lesions.
A very common fungal disease affecting tomatoes, typically starting on older foliage near the ground and displaying characteristic concentric target rings.
Late blight is a fast-moving, destructive oomycete disease capable of killing mature tomato plants and rotting entire fruit trusses within one to two weeks during wet conditions.
Healthy tomato foliage with deep green leaflets, strong aromatic scent, active vegetative growth, and no signs of bacterial specks, blights, or viruses.
